notes.text: "Anciently the sound of the trumpet summoned the congregation of Israel before the Lord at the door of the tabernacle. Their response represented a people assembled in a public acknowledgment of Jehovah as their King. This is but the type for the trumpets which will sound calling forth the elect on the day of his coming (Matt. 24: 31), and not only the living but those who have died (1 Corinth. 15: 52; D&C 88: 92)." [Joseph Fielding Mc Conkie, Gospel Symbolism, p. 275.]
I will [show] thee things which must be hereafter. Jesus himself shows John several scenes of heaven (4:2-5:14) and then events that would yet occur upon the earth.

quotes.text: Come up hither. John is commanded to "come up" to the throne room, suggesting an ascension from the holy place to the most holy, as in the structure of the earthly temple. Similarly, Moses was commanded to "come up unto the Lord" (Ex. 19:24) to the mountain sanctuary.
quotes.source: Understanding the Book of Revelation [Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co.
quotes.attr: Donald W. Parry and Jay A. Parry, Understanding the Book of Revelation [Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1998], 57

quotes.text: After this I looked. This formula indicates that a new vision has begun (7:1, 9; 15:5; 18:1; 19:1; Dan. 7:6-7).
quotes.source: Understanding the Book of Revelation [Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co.
quotes.attr: Donald W. Parry and Jay A. Parry, Understanding the Book of Revelation [Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1998], 57

quotes.text: * After this I looked, and behold a door was opened in heaven; and the first voice which 1 heard was as it were of a trumpet talking with me, which said, Come up hither, and I will show thee things which must be hereafter'

notes.text: Commenting on this verse, Elder Mc Conkie explained that "John is seeing what is to be in the future; he is seeing certain elders in celestial splendor who at that time were in their disembodied state in paradise awaiting the day of their resurrection and the receipt of eternal life. In principle it is the same as when Joseph Smith, on January 21, 1836, saw his father and mother--who were then still living in mortality--in the celestial kingdom of heaven. (Joseph Smith, Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, p. 107.)" [DNTC 3: 465.]

notes.text: The symbols listed below are compiled from several sources, including J.C. Cooper, An Illustrated Encyclopaedia of Traditional Symbols, Thames and Hudson. Man Head or Face is Intelligence, Mind and Spirit--Represents Pre-Earthlife and Spirit Child Calf (Ox in Ezekiel) is Service, the Yoke of Christ and Strength--Represents Mortality Lion is Kingship, Judah (David) and Heirship with Christ--Represents Millennium Flying eagle is celestial, ascension, victory, omniscience authority--Resurrection Universally, the eagle is constantly depicted as having victory over the serpent. In Aztec culture, it was symbolic of celestial power.

"In the 'visions of God' which he saw, Ezekiel also spoke of four beasts who had the faces of a man, a lion, an ox (John says a calf), and an eagle. (Ezekiel. 1: 10.) The presumption is that both prophets were seeing some of the same things." [DNTC 3: 468.]

quotes.text: * After this I looked, and behold a door was opened in heaven; and the first voice which 1 heard was as it were of a trumpet talking with me, which said, Come up hither, and I will show thee things which must be hereafter'

Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty. Similarly, when Isaiah envisions the heavenly temple, he witnesses the seraphim honoring God with the threefold repetition "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts" (Isa. 6:3Isa. 6:3). The threefold repetition emphasizes the superlative degree: God is the holiest of all creatures in the universe. Holy speaks concerning the wonderful separateness of God, his distinctiveness in perfection and power.
quotes.source: Understanding the Book of Revelation [Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co.
quotes.attr: Donald W. Parry and Jay A. Parry, Understanding the Book of Revelation [Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Co., 1998], 63
